chapter: San Francisco, the So Different Orchestra and Johnny
title: Why the best clubs were in Watts and Vernon
summary: Liquor was prohibited in Los Angeles but not in the county, so nightclubs sprang up in Watts and Vernon, including Al Levy's Tavern.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: And I think you mentioned off the tape to me earlier about why the clubs...all the best clubs were in Watts...was why?

Well, in Los Angeles, in those days, you couldn't buy liquor in Los Angeles--prohibited in Los Angeles--but it was all right in the county, so your people went to Vernon to nightclubs and they bought their liquor in there, and they went to Watts.
Which was right over the L.A. City line into L.A. County.

In the county, but you couldn't buy it in Los Angeles. So there was another big white fellow named...uh, I think, Marshall or something like that, that had another big nightclub--that had another big restaurant in Los Angeles, and he opened a place in Watts. And there was three or four big white places in Watts. But Baron Long had the place called the Baron Long Taverns, which he took over from Al Levy. Al Levy, before that, built the Tavern, which had a big restaurant in Los Angeles on Third and Main Street, called Al Levy's, and then he built the place in Watts called Al Levy's Tavern but he didn't do so good. Then Baron Long come along and took it over--which Baron Long owned The Ship Cafe at that time.
